title: Relativity, the Surge and a Third Scientific Revolution
content_preview:
Title Relativity, the Surge and a Third Scientific Revolution
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) James E Beichler
Keywords Relativity
Published 2008
No. of pages 14
Abstract
Quantum theory emerged the victor of the last Scientific Revolution even though relativity theory had a more progressive view of reality to offer science. As a result, the physical aspects and properties of the gravitational field were never fully explored or exploited and science went through several decades of denial concerning the relevance of general relativity and its physical implications. The only small victory that relativity theory could claim before the 1960s was in cosmology with the expanding universe. The victory was small because the expanding universe was far from the everyday needs of a science more concerned with the atom and the nucleus. Under these circumstances, the theory of relativity had no practical applications in the everyday real world, so its theoretical implications were largely ignored. However, the 1970s brought something of a resurgence of good fortunes and everyday relevance for relativity theory and quantum theorists finally accepted the possibility that unification was the primary goal of physics, albeit a unification based upon the quantum concept of discrete particles rather than the Einsteinian concept of field continuity: According to quantum field theory, the gravity field could be reduced to an exchange of gravitons. But what at first seemed a resurgence of general relativity under the quantum paradigm in the 1970s has slowly evolved into a surge of physical relevance resulting in the emergence of general relativity as a dominating field of research in physics. And the story does not end there. The recent discoveries of Dark Matter and Dark Energy are about to push physics and relativity theory into a Third Scientific Revolution in which a unification with the quantum will be made on relativity's terms. Title Relativity: a Pillar of Modern Physics or a Stumbling Block

Author(s) Gurcharn S Sandhu
Keywords Relativity , Reference frame, Absolute motion, Spacetime, Mass-energy equivalence.
Published 2011
Volume Proc. of SPIE Vol. 8121
Number 812109
No. of pages 15
Abstract
Currently, the theory of Relativity is being regarded as one of the main pillars of Modern Physics, essentially due to its perceived role in high energy physics, particle accelerators, relativistic quantum mechanics, and cosmology. Since the founding assumptions or postulates of Relativity and some of the resulting consequences confound the logic and common sense, a growing number of scientists are now questioning the validity of Relativity. The advent of Relativity has also ruled out the existence of the 19th century notion of ether medium or physical space as the container of physical reality. Thereby, the Newtonian notions of absolute motion, absolute time, and absolute reference frame have been replaced with the Einsteinian notions of relative motion, relative time, and inertial reference frames in relative motion. This relativity dominated viewpoint has effectively abandoned any critical study or advanced research in the detailed properties and processes of physical space for advancement of Fundamental Physics. In this paper both special theory of relativity and general relativity have been critically examined for their current relevance and future potential. We find that even though Relativity appears to be a major stumbling block in the progress of Modern Physics, the issue needs to be finally settled by a viable experiment [Phys. Essays 23, 442 (2010)] that can detect absolute motion and establish a universal reference frame.

title: Remarks on Foundations of Physics
content_preview:
Title Remarks on Foundations of Physics
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Jozef Kajfosz
Keywords foundations of physics, basic research, causality, visuality, acton model, gas-like ether
Published 2013
No. of pages 10
Abstract
A simple scheme for ordering the facts of physics is presented, and some terms associated with basic research are introduced. Some aspects of this research are discussed and an outline of a simple model as an example of a working hypothesis for explaining the known facts is proposed. <o:p></o:p>
Overview
This ten-page essay is Jozef Kajfosz 's statement of method rather than of physics. Written in Polish in 1980, never submitted to a journal, posted on a web site and translated into English in 2013, it proposes a simple geometrical scheme — a triangle of facts — for ordering everything physics knows, uses that scheme to define what a "basic discovery" would be, states three rules such a discovery would have to satisfy, and then offers a deliberately unfinished model of the unknown as an illustration of what obeying those rules might look like.
Kajfosz's complaint is not that any particular theory is wrong. It is that the questions at the foundations of physics have no institutional home. The philosophy of science handles them so formally that it "does not reach the average physicist"; physicists themselves raise them "rarely and reluctantly," at seminars "regarded to be not fully serious," in popular works, or at jubilees — because "an unwritten social code says that it is necessary to be a physicist of a very high rank in order to be allowed to take up such a subject. But it seems that the opposite should be right."
The second and more distinctive theme is visuality . Kajfosz argues that physics since Maxwell has progressively abandoned demonstrative models in favour of pure description, and that this is a real loss of understanding rather than a maturation. title: Remarks on Photon-Hadron Interactions
content_preview:
Title Remarks on Photon-Hadron Interactions
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) E Comay
Keywords Photon , Hadron, VMD
Published 2003
Journal Apeiron
Volume 10
Number 2
No. of pages 17
Abstract
Theoretical aspects of VMD and related approaches to real photon-hadron interaction are discussed. The work relies on special relativity, properties of linearly polarized photons, angular momentum conservation and relevant experiments. It is explained why VMD and similar approaches should not be regarded as part of a theory but, at most, as phenomenological models. A further experiment pertaining to this issue is suggested.
Overview
E. Comay's 2003 Apeiron paper is a critique of Vector Meson Dominance (VMD) and the family of related ideas he groups together as "Photon's Hadronic Structure Approaches" (PHSA). The experimental facts these approaches were built to explain are not in dispute and Comay states them plainly: the cross section for hard photons scattered from a proton target is practically the same as from a neutron target, and the number of hadrons emitted from a photon–proton interaction region exceeds the leptonic number by four orders of magnitude. Something about the photon's behaviour at high energy is strongly hadron-like and largely independent of the target's electric charge.
What Comay attacks is the theoretical construction erected on top of those facts — the claim that a physical photon is a superposition of a pure electromagnetic component and a hadronic component,
| γ > = c 0 | γ 0 > + c h | h >,
with the fluctuation between the two treated as an inherent property of the photon, independent of its distance from any hadronic target, and the relative time spent in each state given by the squared moduli of the coefficients. In most versions | h > is a neutral vector meson carrying the photon's spin, parity and charge-conjugation quantum numbers; in Gribov's variant it may belong to a larger set of hadronic states.

"Replacing Coulombs with Meters" is an article by Jeff Yee published on 23 March 2019 on Beyond Mainstream .
Yee argues that naming units after Coulomb, Newton, Ampere and Tesla, while a fitting honour, has helped keep the electrical and mechanical domains of physics apart: a student meeting a named unit is less likely to ask what it actually measures. Most such units reduce to simpler SI terms — the ampere to coulombs per second — and he contends that one unit in particular, once simplified, bridges the gap between the two domains.

Replacing Special Relativity By John Hodge was a live session on 6 April 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Re-interpreting the experiments that formed the base of Special Relativity.
Summary
John Hodge supplied a recorded video applying the Scalar Theory of Everything to the observations on which special relativity was built, and intended to answer questions afterwards. His connection failed repeatedly before, during and after the recording; he was never able to speak for more than a few seconds, sent no answers to the chat, and the session was ended early. Roger J Anderton hosted, with Franklin Hu filling in.
The video
Hodge's method is to go back to the nineteenth-century experiments — Fizeau's on the index of refraction of moving water, stellar aberration, and Michelson–Morley — and to read the data rather than the conclusions drawn from them.
Fizeau. Light speed increases with the flow and decreases against it. Hodge calls this carry-along rather than drag: the speed of light depends on the local plenum density, greater density giving greater tension and a higher speed, so a photon moving with the fluid spends more of its time on the relative peak and one moving against it in the relative valley.
Michelson–Morley. Hodge put up the graph from the original paper and made an observation about its shape. The differences are not in the east–west direction, where the result is very nearly null, but in the directions corresponding to the Sun–Moon combination — which, he suggested tentatively, makes the residual a tidal effect rather than a motion-through-the-ether effect, and another instance of carry-along from nearby bodies: the table, the room, the Sun and the Moon. filename: Reproducing the Pioneer 10 Anomaly with a Cosmic Lens.html
title: Reproducing the Pioneer 10 Anomaly with a Cosmic Lens
content_preview:
Title Reproducing the Pioneer 10 Anomaly with a Cosmic Lens
Author(s) Glen W Deen
Keywords Pioneer anomaly, Acceleration, Sun
Published 2007
Journal Proceedings of the NPA
Volume 5
Number 1
Pages 43-45
Abstract
Anderson et al. say: ?We have reported an anomalous, constant acceleration of Pioneer 10 and 11, a = (8.74 "1.33)E-8 cm/s 2 , directed towards the Sun, at distances ~20 - 70 AU." This anomaly can be reproduced by a multi-layer, onion-like, spherical cosmic lens centered on the Sun with an inner radius of 20 AU. If the effect stops at around 70 AU then the lens has eight layers, and the outer radius of the lens is 68.58 AU, and the effective refraction index through the eight layers is 1.000587235. If the effect extends beyond 70 AU, then there are more than eight layers. The innermost layer has a thickness of 3.33 AU and a refraction index of 1.000067963, and the eighth layer has a thickness of 9.79 AU and a refraction index of 1.000155628. The ratios between the volumes of adjacent lens layers is a constant, and that constant is within 0.2% of 4 1/3 . In order to make the volume ratios exactly equal to 4 1/3 , the anomaly error bars need to change from ?1.3300 to ?1.3357. The anomalous acceleration towards the Sun is just the calculated "observed" acceleration minus the Newtonian acceleration. The Newtonian acceleration is simply a = GM/R 2 , where GM is the heliocentric gravitation constant, and R is the radial distance from the Sun to the spacecraft. The calculated "observed" acceleration is just the Newtonian acceleration times the effective index of refraction at the spacecraft's location. The effective index of refraction is the product of the individual layer refraction indexes that are interior to the spacecraft's location.

14th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference (21 May 2007)

filename: Resolving Spacecraft Earth-Flyby Anomalies with Measured Light Speed Anisotropy.html
title: Resolving Spacecraft Earth-Flyby Anomalies with Measured Light Speed Anisotropy
content_preview:
Title Resolving Spacecraft Earth-Flyby Anomalies with Measured Light Speed Anisotropy
Author(s) Reginald T Cahill
Keywords light speed , spacecraft
Published 2008
Journal Progress In Physics
Volume 3
Number July, 2008
Pages 9-15
Abstract
Doppler shift observations of spacecraft, such as Galileo, NEAR, Cassini, Rosetta and MESSENGER in earth flybys, have all revealed unexplained speed "anomalies" - that the Doppler-shift determined speeds are inconsistent with expected speeds. Here it is shown that these speed anomalies are not real and are actually the result of using an incorrect relationship between the observed Doppler shift and the speed of the spacecraft - a relationship based on the assumption that the speed of light is isotropic in all frames, viz invariant. Taking account of the repeatedly measured light-speed anisotropy the anomalies are resolved ab initio. The Pioneer 10/11 anomalies are discussed, but not resolved. The spacecraft observations demonstrate again that the speed of light is not invariant, and is isotropic only with respect to a dynamical 3-space. The existing Doppler shift data also o ers a resource to characterise a new form of gravitational waves, the dynamical 3-space turbulence, that has also been detected by other techniques. The Einstein spacetime formalism uses a special definition of space and time coordinates that mandates light speed invariance for all observers, but which is easily misunderstood and misapplied.

Title Rhysmonic Cosmology
Read in full Link to paper (Internet Archive)
Author(s) Gregory Hodowanec
Published 1985
Read the full paper here (archived copy — the original link is no longer available)
Abstract
Cosmology, in its broadest sense, may be defined as the study of the universe in terms of its origin, its fundamental makeup, and its development in time. Many theories of cosmology have been proposed, and each assumes one or more models by which various phenomena, which are sensed by man or his instruments, are explained. Most of these theories and models are incomplete and thus leave room for alternate theories and explanations. Rhysmonic cosmology is a "new" theory which starts from fundamental premises and therefore builds-up a model of the universe from a firm foundation. It is the aim of this monograph to introduce the reader to these new concepts and to lead the reader in the development of this cosmology in a logical manner. The theory will not only explain much of what is assumed to be known of this universe, but will also develop new knowledge which will lead to testable predictions and perhaps new and fascinating technologies. The theory also provides logical explanations for many present day enigmas, especially those of an astronomical nature. While the author recognizes that this material is yet incomplete, sufficient information and data will be provided to enable many other independent investigations into this new cosmology. The author hopes that many opt to do so.

Ricardo Libertario Carezani (April 11, 1921 – 2016) was an Argentine-American physicist and the originator of Autodynamics (AD), an alternative theory of relativistic mechanics that he proposed as a replacement for Einstein's special and general relativity.
Biography
Carezani was born on April 11, 1921 in Córdoba, Argentina. He entered Tucumán University in 1939 to study electro-mechanical engineering, and from the outset regarded Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity as ill-founded. Around 1940 he came to believe that the "two observers in relative motion" postulate underlying special relativity was redundant; removing that redundancy, he argued, left a theory in which a single observer describes a phenomenon in its own coordinate system. By about 1945, at the age of 24, he considered the foundations of Autodynamics complete.
In 1951 Carezani published his first book on Autodynamics, which he said was immediately blacklisted by Argentina's National Atomic Energy Commission; only about 300 copies were printed. In August 1954 the Buenos Aires daily Crítica (which ceased publication in 1963) published an account of his theory; Carezani recounted that the paper's publisher was warned not to print anything further by him or face being shut down. He attributed the long delay in developing and publicising Autodynamics to this political climate — his struggle, as he put it, was waged against Perón on one side and the Einstein "myth" on the other.
After Argentina's political reopening, Carezani emigrated to the United States around 1979–1981, settling in California, where he worked as a mathematician and physicist. Richard Phillips Feynman (11 May 1918 – 15 February 1988) was an American theoretical physicist, one of the architects of renormalized quantum electrodynamics , and the source of the diagrammatic method that became the working language of particle physics. On this wiki he appears chiefly as the author of arguments that contributors here dispute, and as the physicist whose own doubts about renormalization are most often quoted back at the theory.
Feynman worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, taught at Cornell from 1945 and at Caltech from 1950. Between 1947 and 1949 he, Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga independently produced formulations of quantum electrodynamics in which the divergent integrals of the theory are absorbed into redefinitions of the measured mass and charge of the electron; Freeman Dyson showed the three formulations to be equivalent, and the three shared the 1965 Nobel Prize. Robert E. Var is an American independent theoretical physicist based in Waltham, Massachusetts. Over nearly three decades he developed a programme — beginning with "space-energy theory" and culminating in "hyper-energy theory" — that treats space as a physical, energy-dense medium and seeks to derive gravity, relativity and cosmology from its dynamics.
Scientific work
Var's central idea is that space is not empty but a medium carrying an enormous intrinsic energy density, and that gravity is a local reduction of that density caused by mass — a principle he attributes to a gravitation theorem published by Maxwell in 1864. His first statement of the approach, " On a New Mathematical Framework for Fundamental Theoretical Physics ," appeared in the mainstream journal Foundations of Physics in 1975.
He later expanded it into a hierarchy of gauge-field theories: a velocity-dependent formulation he argues reproduces special relativity , a tensor "Einstein–Maxwell" theory he offers as a quantizable account of gravity, and finally hyper-energy theory , a many-dimensional cosmology in which the universe is a compressible medium of mass-energy with extra compactified dimensions sourced by the flow of time. He presents this framework as accounting for the big bang , cosmic inflation, the elementary-particle spectrum, and the physical nature of time and superstrings. This later work is largely unpublished and lies outside the scientific mainstream.

The Rodin coil is a toroidal winding pattern devised by Marko Rodin , in which the conductor is wound around a torus in a repeating star-like sequence rather than in the usual evenly spaced circular loops. It is one of the most widely replicated devices in the amateur new energy community, and a substantial body of experimental reports on it is catalogued on this wiki.
The winding
A conventional toroidal coil is wound so that successive turns lie side by side around the ring. In the Rodin pattern the winding instead skips a fixed number of positions on each pass, so that the conductor traces a closed star polygon over the surface of the torus and returns to its starting point only after several circuits. The result is that the current paths cross one another at intervals and the turns are not parallel, which is the feature its advocates regard as essential.
Rodin derived the sequence from what he calls vortex-based mathematics , a scheme built on the repeating digit-sum patterns that appear when the numbers 1–9 are doubled repeatedly (1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 5 and back to 1, with 3, 6 and 9 standing apart). He describes the winding as following "the longest free-flowing path of the electron", and identifies the 3–6–9 triad as governing a flux perpendicular to the coil surface.
Claims
Rodin and those following him have attributed a wide range of properties to the coil, including:
an unusually strong and well-collimated magnetic field along the torus axis, described as a toroidal pinch ;
applications to fusion confinement, brushless motors, high-sensitivity antennas and propulsion;
in the stronger versions of the claim, gravitational effects and energy gain.

In March 1989, Roger Stringham of First Gate Energies, in Hawaii, USA pioneered the method of using acoustic cavitation to produce the cold fusion effect. Acoustic cavitation uses ultrasonic waves to create gas bubbles within the heavy water. Stringham was the first to use the term "sonofusion" to describe how this phenomenon creates energy in cold fusion experiments.
This work is not be confused with other experiments in the hot fusion field which also use a form of acoustic cavitation, called "acoustic inertial confinement fusion." The two types of research are markedly different.
The key differences with the cold fusion method, sonofusion, is that the effect is directly related to an as-yet-unknown interaction between heavy water and a host metal, such as palladium. The hot fusion method does not employ a host metal. The other key distinction between the cold fusion and hot fusion method is that the cold fusion method produces no deadly neutron radiation, as occurs in hot fusion. -- Steven B. His work is unusually coherent for an independent programme: a small number of commitments, applied consistently across electromagnetism, particle structure and the conservation laws, and set out across four books and a series of papers. He argued the case in the technical language of classical field theory rather than by analogy, and his most-read paper is addressed directly to what he considered errors in the standard textbooks .
The aether as the one substance
Dishington's starting point is that space and matter are not two things. In The Extended Electron he describes matter and space as disproportionate distributions of the aether — the same substance, differently concentrated — and in Energy and Charge he accounts for energy and charge as distortions of that substance.
His stated method is worth recording, because it explains the shape of everything he wrote:
If there is no picture to illustrate a theory, constructing one and backing it up with a strong, simple-as-possible mathematical representation is the way to get to new technologies in the shortest time.

"SN 1987A and the Neutrino" is a paper by Ricardo L Carezani challenging the neutrino detections associated with the supernova of February 1987 in the Large Magellanic Cloud — the observation generally regarded as the founding event of neutrino astronomy. Carezani sets out seven numbered "facts" against it.
Overview
Carezani begins from a published summary of the evidence: "The coincidence between the two results provides OVERWHELMING evidence that the neutrinos, formed at the instant the supernova's core collapsed, did INDEED come from this star". His objection is first to the form of the argument — "We suppose what we are trying to prove: neutrinos!" — and then to the data behind it.
The argument
The seven facts
Fact 1. Of four detectors then operating, one — Mont Blanc — recorded the first claimed burst, at 02:52:36.8 UT. IMB, Kamiokande II and the South Dakota experiment did not. Twenty-five per cent agreement, Carezani argues, is not overwhelming evidence.
Fact 2. Even granting simultaneity between Mont Blanc and Kamiokande II, two of four detectors saw nothing, so the agreement is at best 50 per cent.
Fact 3. Producing the assumed flux from 180,000 light years away requires converting 10 to 15 per cent of a solar mass to neutrinos. No mechanism for this is supplied, and the mechanism would differ from anything known in stars.
Fact 4. To explain neutrinos arriving at Kamiokande II twelve seconds after the first burst, a "neutrino sphere" some tens of kilometres in radius is invoked to trap and release them. title: Satellite Motion in a Non-Singular Gravitational Potential
content_preview:
Title Satellite Motion in a Non-Singular Gravitational Potential
Author(s) Ioannis Iraklis Haranas , Spiros Pagiatakis
Keywords Non-singular potential, Lagrange planetary, equations, Disturbing potential, Eccentricity functions, Hansen coefficients ? GRACE?
Published 2010
Journal Vixra
Volume Astrophys Space Sci, Volume 3
No. of pages 7
Abstract
We study the effects of a non-singular gravitational potential on satellite orbits by deriving the corresponding time rates of change of its orbital elements. This is achieved by expanding the non-singular potential into power series up to second order. This series contains three terms, the first been the Newtonian potential and the other two, here R1 (first order term) and R2 (second order term), express deviations of the singular potential from the Newtonian. These deviations from the Newtonian potential are taken as disturbing potential terms in the Lagrange planetary equations that provide the time rates of change of the orbital elements of a satellite in a non-singular gravitational field. We split these effects into secular, low and high frequency components and we evaluate them numerically using the low Earth orbiting mission Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE). We show that the secular effect of the secondorder disturbing term R2 on the perigee and the mean anomaly are 4 .307 ? 10−9/a, and −2 .533 ? 10−15/a, respectively. These effects are far too small and most likely cannot easily be observed with today's technology. Numerical evaluation of the low and high frequency effects of the disturbing term R2 on low Earth orbiters like GRACE are very small and undetectable by current observational means

Nobody came into the live room, so Franklin Hu ran what he called a mailbag: reading out the week's email correspondence on the nature of light and answering it, with comments coming in from the stream. The topic had been running all week on the email list: the standard textbook picture of an electromagnetic wave — electric and magnetic vectors at right angles, in phase, propagating through empty space — and whether anything of the sort actually happens. The objections to the picture
Bob had two. The first is energy: square the two fields and add them, and the total goes to zero at the nodes and back to a maximum, which he cannot reconcile with conservation. The second came from his reading of Jefimenko , who argues that Maxwell's equations are not causal. Once retardation is put in properly, a changing electric field does not cause a changing magnetic field, nor the reverse; the charges are the source of both, and the two merely propagate together, which is why they look like cause and effect. He added that the picture omits the longitudinal Coulomb component that an oscillating source charge must produce.
Hu pressed the same point geometrically. If there is a source, the field should fall off as the inverse square, which the picture does not show; and the only way to get vectors pointing uniformly perpendicular, rather than radially from a point, would be a flat charged plate cycling between plus and minus five volts, with a rectangular magnet reversing alongside it. Is it legitimate to question a medical consensus?
Ian put the question that framed the session. Dissidents make a practice of questioning consensus in physics; medicine now presents an international consensus of the same kind, with politicians deferring wholly to it. Is scepticism appropriate here, or irresponsible? His own answer was that the human pressures are identical — careers ended for stepping out of line, funding tied to producing the expected numbers — and that if anything they operate more strongly in a less exact science. He drew a list of what he called secular apocalypses he had lived through: acid rain, the ozone hole, the exhaustion of fossil fuels, Y2K, global warming and then climate change, SARS and Ebola, weapons of mass destruction — each in its turn the end of the world, each questionable only at the sceptic's cost.
Ricker's version was drier: we are at the bottom of the food chain, told to believe the media, which produces experts, who are presumed to know. Whether certified experts can be wrong is the legitimate question, and we cannot tell from here.
Hu's own scepticism was narrower and concrete. He could not reconcile the advice not to wear masks with the effort to secure masks for health workers, nor with other countries handing them out; and the shortages had not eased in weeks. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, James Keene and Cornelis Verhey , with Bill Lucas commenting from the YouTube stream. It started from a small puzzle Ian had been chewing on and ran, by a chain of ordinary steps, to the structure of the vacuum and the Michelson–Gale experiment.
Viscosity, and what it says about mass
Ian's puzzle: liquids grow less viscous as they warm — treacle in January against treacle in June, the oil in an engine — but gases do the opposite, and he had checked it twice, latterly against Jeans's Dynamical Theory of Gases , because it sounded wrong. Nobody in the room could account for the inversion; Hu had expected heat to loosen the bonds in both cases.
Hu's way of thinking about it was mechanical: a rack dragged across a table crowded with billiard balls, the resistance set by how many balls are in the way; add glue to the balls and the sticking matters more when they move slowly, which gives the liquid behaviour. The discussion passed through what distinguishes a solid from a liquid — Hu's criterion being that the bonds hold their geometry regardless of external energy, which is why one solid will not pass through another — and Ian's correction that the state is not a property of the substance, since water takes all three.
That produced the session's key move. If a spoon meets more resistance in molasses than in water, and mass is defined by force over acceleration, then the mass of a marble is not a property of the marble but of the marble against its medium. Hu pressed this deliberately: what he calls matter is the marble; mass is only what we measure when it moves through something.

Summary
David de Hilster hosted a second week in Franklin Hu 's absence, again streaming to both the society's channel and his own Dissident Science , and set the topic deliberately: is charge real?
The case against charge
De Hilster opened with a question few could answer — who first put the plus and minus signs on things? — and gave the answer as Benjamin Franklin. His argument follows from that. The signs are a notation adopted to record which things attract and which repel; they have since become so ingrained that people take charge for an innate property of matter. He regards it instead as a magical attribute imposed on a particle, and asks anyone who uses it for a physical account of what a field actually is. The model he and his father Robert de Hilster are writing up needs no charge at all: the nucleus holds what orbits it for mechanical reasons, everything is Newtonian, and by Occam's razor the burden falls on whoever wants the extra ingredient. He noted that Glenn Borchardt 's neomechanics likewise dispenses with it.
Hu, watching from the road, wrote in twice. First that charge is too complex a phenomenon to be an assumption — which de Hilster read back as an argument for his own side, since an assumption is precisely what one declines to explain. Then that charge needs to emerge as the result of something like ordinary Newtonian physics, at which de Hilster cheerfully declared they agreed.

Keene's Physicist's Survival Guide
Keene opened with the video he is planning: clicking through the physics literature at random and noting what it says. His complaint is not that the accounts are wrong so much as that they contradict each other. Elementary particles are defined as those with no smaller constituents — and then CERN papers openly track the breakdown products of the heavy quarks. Grand unification presumes a weak force which he does not regard as a force at all: on his account the weak interactions all rest on the unconditional bit operation, and calling it a force is like calling rust one. The speed of light is listed as a constant of vacuum, whereas his own work has it varying, and requires a minimum quantity of quanta present for light to be conducted at all.
He also gave his reading of magnetic monopoles, which he says need not be a new kind of particle: on his model the L bits are magnetic monopoles, and the reason a divided bar magnet always yields a north and a south is that the division never gets down to the fundamental length constant.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, James Keene , Bob Gray , Carl and Alex, the whole of it on dark matter. Hu's microphone was barely audible for the first half — a Windows update had reset the level — so Ian carried much of the discussion, and Hu twice handed the chair over while attending to his mother.
Ian: are spiral galaxies spiral?
Ian's proposal, which he has raised before and thinks neglected, is that what we see in the night sky is not a contemporaneous snapshot. An object is visible only if it happened to be at a distance of X light years at the moment X years ago when it emitted the light; if it was elsewhere then, the light has already passed us or has not yet arrived. Looking at a nebula whose near side is a million light years away and whose far side is two million, we are combining events separated by a million years.
From that he draws two conclusions. First, that the gravitational effects attributed to dark matter may simply be matter we cannot see — ordinary matter, of the kind found in a laboratory, that is not at the right distance for its light to reach us now. He prefers to call this dark stuff , declining the mainstream term. Second, and more provocatively, that spiral galaxies may not be spiral. His tentative position is that they are elliptical or spherical bodies whose apparent shape is the composite of parts seen at different epochs as the object rotates.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , James Keene , Bob Gray and a new participant, Toby. The theme was set by Lucas — how to judge between competing theories — and it turned into a sustained cross-examination of his own.
Distinti, and the case for polytheism
Lucas had found a YouTube channel by Robert Distinti, an electrical engineer with a couple of hundred videos, and recommended it as a third party critical of everyone's theories rather than of any one of them. Hu played David de Hilster 's review of Distinti's latest.
The point that stuck was Distinti's rule that a theory's ability does not prove its exclusivity: that a model gives good answers does not show no other model would give the same ones. De Hilster's illustration from his own experience was a dean telling him his thesis was ridiculous because Maxwell's equations are irrefutable — which, he said, misses that there may be another way to arrive at the same place. Distinti's remedy for what he calls polytheism — several theories fitting the same data — is to increase the sampling footprint until the candidates can be told apart, his example being two sine waves of different frequency that both pass through every measured point until one measures more finely.
Lucas drew from it the moral he cared about: a theory is never finished. General relativity was put forward to explain gravity, and when the Pioneer trajectories and the spiral arms did not fit, the response was to add dark matter and dark energy rather than to falsify anything.

Summary
Bob Gray presented an update on his classical electrodynamics research, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene and Alistair Riddoch taking part.
Gray: from Weber to a generalized Maxwell system
Gray is looking for the simplest and most complete route to classical electrodynamics. His starting point is Weber electrodynamics, which is conventionally presented without fields at all: everything follows from a single potential energy function. He has taken that function and defined fields and potentials from it, arriving at four equations that look much like Maxwell's but carry three extra terms. Those terms come from the time derivative of the charge density, which appears in Weber's approach and, for reasons he cannot see, not in Maxwell's; set them to zero and the two systems coincide. He treats this as evidence that Maxwell's system comes up short.
What he wants and cannot yet get is the expression for the electrodynamic field that he was taught comes from special relativity. He would rather not import relativity into Weber to obtain it, and he reported a correction to his own understanding: Heaviside derived that same expression from Maxwell's equations in 1888, seventeen years before the relativity paper, so it does not depend on relativity at all. Lucas's The Universal Force derives it too, from six empirical laws of electrodynamics — more assumptions than Weber's one potential function, which is why Gray keeps looking.

A small chat over the Christmas week — Franklin Hu and Ian Cohen for most of it, joined by James Keene and, on a poor line, Harry Ricker . It was given over almost entirely to Ian's report of attending a public lecture on the 1919 eclipse expeditions, and to what he learned there.
Ian at Astronomy Ireland
Ian had gone to a lecture by Professor Peter Coles of Maynooth, given to Astronomy Ireland, on the centenary of the Eddington–Dyson eclipse measurement. He asked from the floor why no terrestrial experiment had been contemplated, and then put his own position: that general relativity as such — the space-time account — has not been verified, only certain peripheral anomalies. Coles replied that if one neglects all the evidence then of course there is no evidence, and the audience applauded. Ian's own description of the moment was fair to both sides: the speaker had said all the right things about science being open to question, was not hostile, and was courteous afterwards in the pub, but was plainly reluctant to engage, and the applause was for putting down a crank at the back.
He pressed two further points privately. On the standard rejoinder that GPS confirms general relativity daily, he answered that what GPS shows is the variation of atomic clock rates with gravitational potential, which is not general relativity as such; and he said that GPS contradicts special relativity, since the speed of light there is not independent of the observer's motion. He got no reply to the second.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Alistair Riddoch , Ian Cohen, James Keene , Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker and Toby. It began with Riddoch's model of the vacuum and turned into an argument about what would count as doing science at all.
Infinity, and immutability
Riddoch opened with two things he had been turning over. The first was density: he had learned that relativity has the centre of a black hole infinitely dense, and wanted to know whether infinite density is even a possible thing. Hu's answer was that an infinity in a result is a red flag that something has gone wrong, and he made the same complaint about renormalization, which he calls dividing one infinity by another and keeping the answer. Ian agreed — thou shalt not divide by zero — and extended it to the big bang's infinitely small interval and infinitely great density, and to the Copenhagen picture, which appears to require an infinite speed of transmission where relativity has a finite one.
The second was the word immutable . Riddoch's own model has Planck-scale building blocks that have always existed and never change: not permeable, not compressible, not flexible. What changes is only their relative orientation, spin polarity and rate of rotation. Because they are not perfect spheres — their surfaces are wave-deformed — the gaps between them do change, alternating between hyperbolic tetrahedra and hyperbolic octahedra as the blocks turn. Those gaps are genuine void, with no properties at all except a shape, and the shape is defined entirely from outside: as he put it, it is the doughnut that defines the hole, not the hole.

Eugene: a biogenic origin for earthquakes
Eugene presented what he calls the biogenic earthquake hypothesis, posted as a preprint on EarthArXiv: that microbial life beneath the surface may trigger earthquakes.
His argument runs in stages. The accepted limit on the depth of the biosphere — twelve to fifteen kilometres — rests on temperature and pressure limits he thinks badly underestimated: the most extreme organism known before 2018 tolerated 122 to 130 °C, and a strain found that year survives well beyond it. Set against models of the earth's interior composition, he arrives at a possible limit near seventy-five kilometres, which is deep enough to matter for earthquakes.
For how such organisms would feed, he pointed to a documented case: bacterial chains beneath the ocean floor that perform a distributed respiration, the deeper cells taking electrons from sulphur and passing them up the chain to cells at the surface that attach them to oxygen — effectively feeding on an electric current. He suggests telluric currents could do the same tens of kilometres down. He also gave energy estimates that he says are adequate even for a magnitude nine event.

Keene's density ranges
Keene reported extending an earlier study by parsing the whole range of initial quanta density in his simulator, from absolute vacuum — no one-state bits at all — up to maximum, where every locus is occupied. The ranges he now identifies: above about 0.75 a lepton–quark soup; between roughly 0.66 and 0.75, plasma; and below that, down to about 0.1, the range in which atoms occur. He noted that the higher end of the atomic range appears to favour higher- Z atoms, which he takes as consistent with the astrophysical account of heavy elements forming in large explosions.
Hu queried that immediately, and the question was a good one: if all atoms are made of the same protons, neutrons and electrons, why should their bit density differ? Keene did not evade it but did not settle it either; his answer went by way of the simulation's behaviour rather than the chemistry.
Run in vacuum mode, anything with momentum leaves the volume and is lost, so the volume cools to what he calls absolute zero — no radiation out, no particle motion — a state unreachable in the laboratory but exact in simulation. Bob Gray presented on the internal consistency of Maxwell's equations, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker , James Keene , Cornelis Verhey , Carl and, later, David de Hilster .
Gray's claim
Gray had been working from Frederick David Tombe 's account of Maxwell's original equations, drawn from the 1861 and 1864 papers — twenty equations, presented in vector notation as eight. His question is not whether the equations agree with experiment but whether they are mathematically consistent among themselves: can one show, for a given equation, that the left-hand side genuinely equals the right?
To ask that he had to add assumptions, which he listed and offered for challenge: vacuum permittivity and permeability, one constitutive relation Tombe omits, point charges as an adequate approximation to their positions, the charge density as a sum of delta functions, the current density as charge density times a velocity, and expressions for the scalar and vector potentials for discrete charges. Everything then stands in fundamental quantities and the check can be made.
His result: it fails. Working out the divergence of E with those substitutions yields, on the right, a term containing the accelerations of the charges — the vector potential involves the current density, hence velocity, hence a time derivative giving acceleration — and there is nothing corresponding on the left. So the two sides cannot be equal in general.

The two laboratory methods — the bottle and the beam — do not agree: the beam gives about nine seconds longer than the bottle, against a lifetime near fourteen and a half minutes. If both are equally valid and give different answers, what is being measured? He returned to this as his standing test case, alongside the gravitational constant. He also noted how remarkable the number itself is: fourteen minutes is an age for a subatomic particle, closer to the decay of an atomic nucleus than to a muon. And he explained why the measurement is hard at all: a free neutron is nearly undetectable, and a detector is essentially a counter tube wrapped in a large block of wax, registering what the neutrons produce rather than the neutrons.

From the clocks it went to time itself and stayed there.
Is time quantized?
Keene holds that space, time and energy are all quantized, and that this is what makes his binary mechanics work: with those three quantities discrete, the quantities usually presented to students as fundamental physical constants become derivable rather than merely measured. He put the criterion plainly — by their fruits ye shall know them — and treated the quantization as a postulate justified by its utility, declining to go behind it. Asked why the world should be quantized, he said that is where science shades into philosophy and religion, and that he would leave it to others; he noted that Bill Lucas , asked the same, answers that God made it so, and that this is not where he himself will go.
Hu wanted a physical cause rather than a postulate, and offered one: that we are inside a computer. Nothing in a computer happens faster than the clock; each tick fixes a state; a bit is here or there and never half-way. Keene was sympathetic but said this is only another way of saying that space, time and energy are quantized.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu , with Dennis Allen , Harry Ricker , Ian Cohen and others, running on two threads: what a photon is, and how the earliest radio detector worked.
The shape of the photon
Hu repeated the claim he had made the previous week — that a photon occupies the space of a rod, still a compression wave, with the rod's orientation carrying the polarisation — and drew from it the distinction he thinks matters. At the high-frequency end everything looks like particles; at the radio end everything looks like waves; and that, he argued, is not a continuum of behaviour but two different things. Light generated by atomic electron transitions comes in these rod-like packets of fixed energy; a radio wave is more like an ocean wave, broad and of any amplitude.
Harry Ricker pressed the obvious objection: the electromagnetic spectrum appears continuous, from the very low frequencies once used to reach submerged submarines up to the extreme high frequencies — so where does one behaviour stop and the other begin? Hu's answer was that the boundary is technological, set by how fast electrons can be made to oscillate in a circuit, and he asked repeatedly what the highest radio frequency actually achievable is and where it sits on the spectrum. Ricker's own answer was that the spectrum is one thing described by two different models at the two ends, that the choice is a matter of which model one is using, and that this does not answer what either a photon or a radio wave physically is.

What is wrong with QED
Bob's summary of the paper's complaint was mathematical. Any QED calculation runs into infinities, and what is done with them depends on how the sums are taken and what is subtracted from what. The paper's first equation is the assignment of −1/12 to the sum of all the positive integers — traceable, through its references, to Euler — and this is used in the course of a calculation held up as physics' most accurate. Hu made the same complaint about renormalization: dividing infinity by infinity and keeping the answer.
The session then worked through the encyclopaedia articles on quantum electrodynamics, the quantum vacuum and the anomalous magnetic moment, reading them aloud. Hu could make nothing of the Feynman diagram — an electron and positron annihilating to a gamma ray which then produces a quark, an antiquark and a gluon, three things he takes not to exist — and said it looked like a cartoon.
Keene's objection went to the physics rather than the arithmetic. Most of what is going on, he said, is hidden in the diagram's vertices: when he derives Planck's constant from first principles it comes out as an elemental action divided by the fine structure constant, which implies well over a hundred events inside what is treated as a single Planck-constant event.

Summary
A general science chat hosted by Franklin Hu , standing in with no speaker scheduled, and used to make the first public presentation of an idea he had arrived at two or three months earlier. He stated it without preamble: the shape of a photon is a rod.
Why a shape at all
Hu's argument for insisting on one is that he is a physicalist — if it cannot be shown on a billiard table he does not believe it — and that the history of the DNA molecule is the model. The components were known long before anyone found the arrangement that fitted the data, and the helix ended the mystery. He wants the same for light rather than talk of a photon whose shape nobody will state.
A rod that is a wave
His second claim is that light is strictly a wave: he does not accept wave–particle duality, and says so rather than working around it. What he means by a rod is the wavelet one would get by dipping a rectangular object into a very narrow wave tank — a single pulse with a fixed width and height travelling in a straight line, not the great circular waves one normally makes.
He listed the properties this has to account for: light travels in rays, it does not disperse, and it is localised. His example was pair annihilation, where two back-to-back gamma rays strike specific spots in a silicon detector rather than smearing across it. A rod, he argued, has all three particle-like properties and remains a wave.
The inverse square law he handled by distinguishing the individual photon from the population: a photon from Alpha Centauri arrives at full amplitude, and it is only the number per unit area that thins with distance.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene and Bob Gray , most of it a sustained and good-tempered argument between Hu and Keene about what counts as an explanation.
Deriving the constants
Keene's claim for binary mechanics is that it derives what are called the fundamental constants — the speed of light, Planck's constant, the electron mass and others — from first principles, and that nobody else does. His first principles he described as minimal: the full quantisation of space, time and energy, quantisation being already accepted for charge.
The distinction he insisted on, and which Hu eventually accepted as a clean statement of where they differ, is between deriving a constant and showing interrelationships among constants. The literature is full of formulae relating the fine structure constant, the charge, the speed of light and the rest to one another, and Keene has no quarrel with that work — it is simply, as he put it, a different cage in the zoo. His rule is that unexplained data may not be explained by reference to other unexplained data. He noted, as support rather than opposition, that the standard model concedes it cannot derive any of these constants from its own principles.
Hu's counter, pressed several times, was that binary mechanics grounds out the same way one level down: it takes fundamental quantities of length, time and mass, and cannot say where those come from. Keene agreed without embarrassment — he has not attempted to, and there is an empty slot for anyone who wants to. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Bob, Roger, Bill Lucas , Alistair Riddoch and Ian Cohen, taking up an argument running on the society's email list.
Do a heavy and a light object really fall together?
Ian Cohen set out the case, carefully and at length, that they do not quite. The textbook derivation cancels the small mass from both sides and leaves the acceleration as GM/r ²; but the earth is not stationary, and the object attracts it too, so the relative acceleration is G(M+m)/r ². Two consequences follow. The heavier object accelerates very slightly faster. And, if the two experiments are run one after the other, the heavier object has slightly less distance to cover, because the earth has moved further to meet it. He was emphatic that this is not Aristotle vindicated — the difference is of the order of the object's mass to the earth's — but that it is not exactly zero either.
Hu accepted the distance argument readily and resisted the acceleration one, on the ground that inertial resistance rises in proportion to the force. Ian took him through it again, and the disagreement did not resolve.
Riddoch made the observation that clarified the case: if both objects are released at the same moment, the earth's movement toward them is common to both, so that effect drops out and only the acceleration difference remains — which is exactly the thought experiment Ian had proposed. He then scaled it up memorably: if the whole human population jumped a metre at once, the earth would move about a twelve-trillionth of a metre the other way, and when one person alone jumps, it moves eight billion times less.

The disagreement
Gary's position, as Hu set it out from the video, is that light is strictly a particle: photons drawn as circles, with the polarisation an inherent property of each, no waves anywhere, and radio behaving the same way. Hu's is that a photon is a wavelet in a medium.
Hu was at pains to say how much he agrees. Treating photons as discrete clumps travelling through space with a definite volume and length is right; so is the account of what they do on arrival, jostling electrons; so is the photoelectric explanation, that what matters is the energy delivered per unit time rather than the total, with the fixed quantum hv per packet. His own picture of the photon as a rod maps onto Gary's circles, the rod's orientation supplying the polarisation.
His criticism is that the account is incomplete rather than wrong: it has to postulate a photon that stands in no relation to anything else known, and cannot say what it is made of. He used his standing image for this — the socks disappearing from the dryer, which little elves would explain perfectly consistently and without any way of being tested. Logical consistency, he said, is grossly insufficient. His own theory, he argued, sits one level below Gary's and says what the clump is.

Bob's answer: there is no magnetic field
Bob's case, developed over a long presentation, is that the magnetic field is not a physical field at all.
He began with terminology — field means several different things, and if one defines an electrodynamic field as force per unit charge on a test body, then B does not qualify, its units being wrong.
His alternative comes from Weber electrodynamics, where the force between two charged bodies is the Coulomb force multiplied by a coupling coefficient with a constant term, a velocity-dependent term and an acceleration-dependent term. His analogy was static against kinetic friction: nobody finds it strange that the coupling between two objects differs according to their relative motion. On this reading the magnetic field is simply that dynamic coupling, and the Coulomb field is the only real physical field.
He applied Occam's razor twice. First to William J Hooper , who identifies three electric fields — Coulomb, motional and transformer — which Bob tabulated to show that they differ precisely in how many time derivatives they carry: none, one, two. Second to the multipole expansion of the scalar potential, whose infinite series of terms would, on the same logic, give an infinite series of fields.

Method
He began with what he thinks goes wrong. Where hands-on experiment is possible, results repeat; the earth and the universe do not allow it, and the strongest evidence is where laboratory work backs the theoretical construct. So one should question any proposed esoteric law that has no empirical verification, and remember that a concept being visualisable does not make it obey the laws of physics.
He then defined worldview as what the scientist brings to the table — the paradigms absorbed from classes and books. These are two-edged: without a framework we could not make sense of anything, and with one we cannot see past it. To a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

Abstract
A new cosmological theory is presented based on the proposition that all four metrical coefficients of space and time change with the cosmological expansion. Such a universal scale expansion would preserve the four-dimensional spacetime geometry and therefore by general relativity most physical relationships. In addition, if the scale expansion were exponential with time, all epochs would be equivalent. The argument
Keene's paper takes its stand on a remark of Bell's own: that there is a way to escape the inference of superluminal speeds and spooky action at a distance, but that it involves absolute determinism. That escape is the freedom loophole , and Keene's claim is that binary mechanics occupies it — a local realist theory with exact time development laws, in which all action occurs over one length constant in one time constant, and in which the one-state quanta exist whether observed or not.
The consequence he draws is that entanglement experiments cannot settle the matter by themselves. Closing every other loophole leaves this one; to close it one would have to falsify the local realist theory directly — that is, falsify the quantisation of space, time and energy.
He was scathing about how the loophole is discussed, and this was the liveliest part of the paper: not merely deterministic but super -deterministic; not merely determinism but absolute determinism; not merely hard to imagine but impossible; not merely a question about free will but a loss of freedom to choose ; not merely a new question but unscientific. He called the vocabulary a propaganda ploy — believe in superluminal effects or be an anti-freedom jerk — and said the reason for it is precisely that the experiments alone cannot exclude the alternative.

Lucas on why
Lucas's answer was historical and political. He traced it to the American settlement between the established colonial churches and the revival movements, and argued that from about 1850 the separation of church and state was used to license a science defined by opposition to religion: what Maxwell and Ampère had called the Spirit of God became the electric field, and quantum mechanics took the universal wave function rather than the field as its object. He credited Poincaré with a meta-theory of theorems from logic applicable to all scientific theories, said Poincaré published relativity a year before Einstein and then showed by those theorems that it was false, and that this was why the theory was carried elsewhere.
He gave his own experience as evidence of the cost. Upon comparison of meaning in science method and theory as it is necessarily rooted to common perceptional experience, it is proposed that established criteria of virtual, real, and actual employed for description in internet studies not only constitute 'world', but 'universe' in which the gap between the actual and virtual has a physical meaning. Scott A. Mainwaring is an American consultant and philanthropist based in Helena, Montana, who is known within Electric Universe circles as a principal supporter and co-founder of the SAFIRE Project, an experimental effort to test the Electric Sun model.
Biography
Mainwaring resides in Helena, Montana, where he has worked as a consultant and part-time lecturer. He is the son of Bruce Mainwaring, a longtime advocate of the Electric Universe idea, and together they have directed the Mainwaring Archive Foundation, the philanthropic vehicle through which the family has funded independent scientific research.
Mainwaring became involved in Electric Universe research after attending the 2012 Electric Universe conference, where he encountered the proposal of engineer Montgomery Childs to build an apparatus capable of testing the Electric Sun hypothesis empirically.
Work
Mainwaring recognized in Montgomery Childs' proposal a pragmatic, empirical method for testing the Electric Universe hypothesis, and in particular the Electric Sun model. He introduced the proposal to his father, Bruce Mainwaring, and the two decided to support the initiative through the Mainwaring Archive Foundation.
The resulting effort became the SAFIRE Project, which sought to reproduce and study, in the laboratory, plasma conditions resembling those proposed for the Sun. The project proceeded through a bench-top proof-of-concept phase, a full-scale laboratory phase built around the "SAFIRE Plasma Engine," and subsequent research into the molecular and atomic-scale reactions observed in its plasma environments. Beyond financing the work, Mainwaring consulted regularly with Childs and contributed hands-on assistance during construction of the Phase 2 apparatus.
The SAFIRE Project was later carried forward as a commercial enterprise under Aureon Energy Ltd.

Should Spacetime be Discarded? was a live session presented by Roger J Anderton on 4 May 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
There are problems unifying Einstein's relativity with quantum physics as is well-known. One proposal for unifying them is to discard spacetime. Introducing spacetime into modern physics has created many problems.
Summary
Roger J Anderton hosted this himself, continuing from his sessions on Minkowski spacetime. The question is whether adding spacetime to physics was a mistake, and his angle is that the answer is now being given inside the mainstream as well as outside it: one proposal for unifying relativity with quantum theory is to discard spacetime altogether.
His framing is the historical one he uses repeatedly. The 1905 paper contains no spacetime; Minkowski added it in 1908; general relativity followed in 1915; and between those dates the theory turned into something else. He cited Alexander Unzicker as holding that the development went wrong in exactly that decade.
Two videos
The first was Sabine Hossenfelder on whether gravity is a force, played to set out the position he disputes. title: Sloan Digital Sky Survey
content_preview:
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( SDSS ) is a long-running imaging and spectroscopic survey of the sky, begun in 2000 and named for the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, which funded it. It is the source of much of the observational material that arguments about redshift , quasars and large-scale structure have been conducted on for the past twenty-five years — including a number of the arguments recorded on this wiki.
This article is a short account of the survey oriented to that use. It describes what SDSS is and where it now stands, and then sets out the particular data products that pages on this wiki draw on, and what the disputes over them have been.
The survey
SDSS observes with two telescopes: the Sloan Foundation 2.5 m telescope at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, which has carried the survey since the beginning, and the du Pont 2.5 m telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, which extends it to the southern sky.
Its work divides into two kinds. Imaging records the positions, brightnesses and colours of objects; the imaging camera was retired in 2009, by which time the survey had photometered several hundred million objects over roughly a third of the sky. Spectroscopy — now the whole of the survey's activity — measures the spectrum of a selected object, which is what yields a redshift and hence, on the standard interpretation, a distance.
The survey has run in five phases:
SDSS-I (2000–2005) — the original imaging and redshift survey
SDSS-II (2005–2008) — adding a Milky Way structure survey and the Sloan Supernova Survey
SDSS-III (2008–2014) — including BOSS, the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
SDSS-IV (2014–2020) — extending to the southern hemisphere
SDSS-V (2020– ) — the current phase, organised as three "mappers": the Milky Way Mapper , the Black Hole Mapper (a time-domain spectroscopic survey of quasars and X-ray sources) and the Local Volume Mapper

The Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics (SAA) was founded in 1994 in Southern California by David de Hilster , Dr. Ricardo Carezani , Amnon Meyers and others, with the purpose of advancing the theory of Autodynamics as developed by Carezani. It later had a chapter in the United Kingdom, and it remains the publisher of essentially the whole Autodynamics literature.
Activities
Publishing
The Society produced a book early on but sold only a few copies. The 1998 book was the first to be mass-printed, putting copies into the thousands.
Beyond the books, the Society publishes Carezani's papers, derivations and expository notes at autodynamics.org . That collection is indexed at Ricardo L Carezani and grouped by subject at Autodynamics ; it includes the derivations ( Frames Derivation , Galilean Simplification , The Superfluous System ), the decay papers ( Muon Decay and Autodynamics , Pion Decay and Autodynamics , Nucleus-Nucleus Collision , The Compton Effect and Autodynamics ), the gravitational programme ( Universal Gravitation in Autodynamics and its four applications), and the neutrino papers ( Origin of the Neutrino , Super-Kamiokande: Super-Proof for Neutrino Non-existence , Neutrinos at Fermi Lab , SN 1987A and the Neutrino ).
Several members appear as authors or editors across that body of work: Lucy Haye as co-author of the astrophysical papers, de Hilster and Meyers as editors, and Brian F. Hall as editor of the Pioneer paper.

It is not a paper proposing an alternative model. Spacetime curvature is the proposal, central to general relativity , that gravitation is not a force acting between bodies but a property of the geometry through which they move. Mass and energy deform a four-dimensional continuum of space and time; bodies then follow the straightest available paths through that deformed geometry, and what Newton described as an attractive force appears as an artefact of the shape of the arena.
It is the single most disputed idea documented on this wiki. Roughly 184 pages engage with it directly — some 84 papers, 44 scientist biographies and 14 books — and around 450 discuss curvature in some form. That places it above push gravity , tired light and the Casimir effect in the volume of material collected here.
What the standard account claims
Albert Einstein 's field equations relate the curvature of spacetime at a point to the energy and momentum present there. The account is economical: one geometric statement replaces both the gravitational force and the flat background of special relativity, and it has passed every precision test put to it, from the perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of starlight to the Shapiro delay, gravitational redshift, frame dragging, the orbital decay of binary pulsars and the direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015.
Its critics do not generally dispute those measurements. What they dispute is the interpretation — whether geometry is the cause of gravitation or merely an efficient bookkeeping for it.

Special relativity is the physical theory published by Albert Einstein in 1905 in the paper On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies . It describes the relationship between space and time for observers moving uniformly relative to one another, and it replaced the Galilean transformations of classical mechanics with the Lorentz transformations . Special relativity is also the single most-discussed subject on this wiki. It is the keyword of more papers catalogued here than any other concept in physics, and the literature indexed under it — several hundred papers, together with dozens of books — is overwhelmingly critical. The critics are not a single school. They disagree with each other about what is wrong, about what should replace the theory, and about whether anything need replace it at all. What they share is the conviction that the theory's two postulates, its derivation, its treatment of time and simultaneity, or its claimed experimental support will not survive careful examination. This article states the theory briefly and then presents that body of work, author by author and argument by argument.

The speed of light in vacuum, written c , is the most heavily loaded constant in modern physics. It fixes the ratio between mass and energy, sets the scale of the electromagnetic field equations, defines the metre, and — in the form of Einstein's second postulate, that c has the same value in every inertial frame regardless of the motion of the source — supplies the foundation on which special relativity is built. Since the 1983 redefinition of the SI metre, c is no longer measured at all: it is defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, and the metre is derived from it.
The literature collected on this wiki treats almost every part of that account as open. The researchers documented here do not agree with one another — some hold that c is constant but relative to a medium or a field rather than to every observer; some that the two-way speed is constant while the one-way speed is not; some that c varies with gravitational potential, with the medium, or with time; some that the constancy observed in experiments is an artefact of the instruments used to measure it; and a few that the light-speed barrier can be exceeded outright. What they share is the conviction that the second postulate was elevated to a principle before the experimental evidence could bear it, and that the 1983 redefinition has since made the question difficult even to ask, because a discrepant measurement now registers as a wrongly calibrated metre rather than as a physical result.
This article states the orthodox position, then organises the objections found in the archive by the idea at stake rather than by author.

Abstract
The speed of light according to the Special Theory of Relativity has the same value C with respect to any inertial frame of reference in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space. An attempt to build an alternative physical model in 3-dimensional Euclidean space brings up a question: in what frame of reference does light move with the speed C? Series of experiments and mathematical reasoning suggest that: 1) the speed of a photon emitted by an atom equals to C if measured with respect to the atom if the atom is at rest or moving with a constant speed with respect to a 3-dimensional inertial frame of reference; 2) the speed of light acquires the value of a constant C near Earth, Sun and other large masses; the energy of the photon depends on the gravitational potential, 3) light has inertial properties.
Overview
Presented at the 20th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference in 2013, this paper by Nina Sotina and Nadia Lvov asks a question that special relativity dissolves rather than answers: if space is ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space and time is independent of it, then with respect to what does light travel at c ?
Their answer is a modified emission theory. Light leaves an atom at speed c relative to that atom — Walther Ritz's ballistic hypothesis of 1908 — but does not keep that speed. As it propagates it undergoes what the authors call hidden dynamics : its velocity relaxes toward c in the frame of any large nearby mass, and does so without any loss of energy, the change in speed being compensated by a change in the photon's mass. The relativistic kinematics of Minkowski space is then, on this view, a formalism that gets the right answers by encoding a real dynamical process it does not name.

Stanislav V. Adamenko is a Ukrainian physicist and the founder and scientific director of the Electrodynamics Laboratory "Proton-21" in Kiev, established in 1999.
Work
The laboratory's programme is the pursuit of extreme compression of matter in a small-scale terrestrial apparatus, with the aim of reaching densities approaching those of nuclear matter — conditions Adamenko describes as "stellar" and compares to the interiors of white dwarfs and neutron stars.
The method is a pulsed electron beam of up to a kilojoule, at a few hundred keV and lasting tens of nanoseconds, directed at a solid target a few tens of micrometres across. Adamenko's claim is that this acts as a "coherent driver", initiating a self-organising and self-sustaining collapse of the electron–nucleus plasma, and that the collapse produces a wholesale nuclear rearrangement of part of the target: the synthesis of elements across the whole periodic table, the creation of superheavy nuclei beyond any known element, and the conversion of radioactive nuclei into stable ones. The last of these is presented as a possible route to the treatment of nuclear waste.
The work is set out at length in Controlled Nucleosynthesis: Breakthroughs in Experiment and Theory (Springer, 2007), edited with Vladimir Vysotskii and Andrei Vysotskyy, which collects the laboratory's experimental reports and its theoretical account of the collapse. The programme has been presented mainly at the International Conference on Cold Fusion and Condensed Matter Nuclear Science meetings.
The central experimental claims — in particular the detection of stable nuclei with mass numbers between 250 and 500, and the assertion that a milligram of target material undergoes complete nuclear regeneration in each shot — have not been reproduced elsewhere.

Steady state theory is the cosmological model in which the universe has no beginning and no end, presenting on the large scale the same appearance at every epoch, with new matter created continuously to keep the mean density constant as the universe expands.
The standard account
The theory was put forward in 1948 in two papers in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society : one by Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold , the other, on a different formal basis, by Fred Hoyle . Its governing assumption is the perfect cosmological principle — the universe is homogeneous and isotropic not only in space, as ordinary cosmology assumes, but also in time. There is therefore no privileged epoch, no "early universe," and no origin event.
The model accepted the observed expansion. To keep the perfect cosmological principle in the face of expansion, matter must appear continuously; the required rate is very small, of the order of one hydrogen atom per cubic metre every billion years, far below any rate that could be detected directly. The universe is thus infinitely old, infinitely extended, and always the same in the mean, with galaxies of every age present everywhere at every time.
The steady state model was the principal rival to the evolving hot-origin cosmology through the 1950s and early 1960s. It was Hoyle who gave the rival theory its name, using the phrase "big bang" dismissively in a 1949 BBC broadcast. The model was falsifiable in a way its rival was not: because it forbids evolution, any evidence that the distant — and therefore earlier — universe differs systematically from the nearby one counts directly against it. The theory predicts that a collapsing star will expand again, and continue to alternately expand and collapse at a rate depending on the mass and greatest radius of the star. The star collapses, turbulence and rotation halt the infall, it re-expands to nearly its original radius, and the cycle repeats, shedding matter and radiation each time. The book asks why a handful of scientists — Stephen Hawking and Albert Einstein foremost among them — become world-famous figures, and argues that their fame has little to do with the substance of their science. Steven B. Bryant is an American researcher and technology executive known for a mathematical critique of the derivations underlying special relativity, and for the alternative framework he calls Modern Mechanics (or Modern Classical Mechanics).
His central technical claim concerns Einstein's Spherical Wave Proof . Bryant argues that the proof establishes only that the transformed coordinates satisfy the general equation of a sphere, not that they lie on the same sphere — and that when the radii are checked, the transformed points turn out to lie on multiple spheres rather than one. Since the purpose of the proof is to establish the relationship between the constancy of the speed of light and the principle of relativity, he concludes that the relationship is not established.
His positive proposal turns on a distinction he says relativity conflates: length versus wavelength . On his account time dilation, length contraction and the twin paradox are all artefacts of using a length-based model to interpret wavelength-based observations, and he reports that equations built on the distinction fit the Michelson-Morley and Ives-Stilwell results substantially more closely than the Einstein-Lorentz equations do.
Bryant was a subject matter leader in the relativity community of the Natural Philosophy Alliance , has spoken at AAAS (American Association for the Advancement of Science) and NPA conferences at universities across the United States, and set out his framework for a general readership in Disruptive: Rewriting the Rules of Physics (2016). Steven Dinowitz is an American independent theorist, the author of Field Distortion Theory — an attempt to keep the Galilean transformations while still accounting for the experimental evidence usually taken to establish special relativity .
He is worth attention for a reason that has nothing to do with whether the theory is right. In 1991 he derived from it a specific, numerical, dated prediction about a named experiment — that CERN's Large Electron–Positron collider would prove unable to accelerate an electron past 60 GeV. The machine was built, it ran for nine years, and the prediction can be checked.
Field Distortion Theory
The theory begins with light propagation. Dinowitz proposes that the electric field surrounding a source undergoes an "aerodynamic-like distortion" when the source moves through a gravitational field . The distortion, not a change in the structure of space and time, is what produces the observed behaviour of light; the Galilean transformations are retained throughout, and the theory is offered as consistent with the existing optical evidence while suggesting new experiments.
From there he makes the move the rest depends on: a body's inertial mass is a consequence of that same field distortion . Mass therefore does not increase with velocity as such, but with velocity relative to whichever gravitational field is locally dominant in energy density — near the Earth's surface, the Earth's own field.
